----------
howdy, it’s Barsee again.

happy wednesday, AI family, and welcome back to AI Valley.

**here are the biggest things worth knowing today:**

* Anthropic says self-improving AI may be closer than we think

* Google will turn off search for schools that reject AI

* DeepSeek wants AI agents to manage themselves

* People are reverse engineering big software with Opus 5.5

* Plus trending AI tools, posts, and resources

Let’s _dive_ into the Valley of AI…


----------

----------
#### **ATLASSIAN**

## If 87% of devs code faster with AI, why aren't projects shipping faster?

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/21fe9af5-0f79-4ed8-9a2a-8c530ea05b8e/Email_1160x620px_Option02_A__1_.png?t=1793353227)
Caption: Courtesy: Atlassian

Answer the question everyone’s asking right now with Atlassian’s help. 

If you’re managing software developer teams, you’ve probably noticed the friction. Teams are working harder and coding faster, but organizational bottlenecks remain. AI is speeding up individual coding, while information searches, meetings, and context switching remain unchanged.

Atlassian’s 2026 State of Developer Experience report surveyed 1,500+ developers and leaders. The findings? **87% of developers say they’re writing code and shipping faster, but only 28% feel less organizational friction.**

As AI writes more code, developers’ roles are shifting toward intent, architecture, systems thinking, and validation. To unlock AI’s full productivity potential, teams need an AI-native SDLC that tackles these bottlenecks.

Join Andrew Boyagi, Customer Chief Technology Officer at Atlassian, alongside industry thinkers Kelsey Hightower, Jennifer Riggins, and Nathen Harvey on November 9 for a research-backed webinar on building an AI strategy that reduces friction and creates workflows that actually work.

[Register today](https://fandf.co/4zXql6g).

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/244a0640-d3c5-401a-a2a6-9fbe2c7f0d9b/antrss__1_.png?t=1793801291)
Caption: Courtesy: Anthropic

**1/ **[**Anthropic says self-improving AI may be closer than we think.**](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026068676/anthropicpbc-sx1ax1.htm) Its IPO filing has a line I had to read twice: future Claude models may soon reach the point where AI dramatically speeds up AI research. That’s the milestone people tie to recursive self-improvement, or RSI.

Claude already helps Anthropic run experiments, generate training data, write code and evaluate new models. Fine, we knew that. What caught me was Anthropic admitting it has missed significant speed-ups in its own development before, and only noticed after they’d happened.

No current Claude model has crossed that threshold, and Anthropic isn’t claiming AI can build its successors without humans. It’s also a risk disclosure, the section where companies list everything that could go wrong, not a product announcement.

But [Sundar Pichai was talking about RSI](https://x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/2115546957909533157) just days ago, and now Anthropic is putting it in front of investors. Two rival labs raising the same possibility is notable on its own. One of them saying it might not see it coming is the part I can’t stop thinking about.

**2/ **[**Google will turn off search for schools that reject AI.**](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/google-search-schools-restrict-ai.html?unlocked_article_code=1.N1E.ptjc.6fOSKNFJlLLf&smid=url-share&utm_source=tldrnewsletter)** **Google is giving schools more control over AI, with an awkward catch. Under its upcoming K-12 settings, Search, Gemini and other AI tools will be off by default until administrators switch them on. But there’s no way to switch on the old, AI-free Google Search.

Google says Search and AI are now too intertwined to separate. So a school that wants no AI loses Google Search too.

The timing isn’t great. New York City and Los Angeles have already restricted student AI use, two US senators have pressed Google over its classroom push, and former FTC chair Lina Khan [accused](https://x.com/linamkhan/status/2117680024216330673) Google of using its search dominance to pressure schools into accepting AI.

Google [insists](https://x.com/NewsFromGoogle/status/2117714815477059722) this gives schools more choice, and technically it does. Administrators can turn on Search without the separate Gemini app. They just can’t get Search without AI. And for schools already running on Chromebooks, Docs and Classroom, walking away from Google isn’t really on the table.

**3/ **[**DeepSeek wants AI agents to manage themselves.**](https://x.com/DeepSeekHarness/status/2116857257245987236) Its new technical write-up introduces Super-agent, an architecture for running lots of AI tasks without babysitting every session.

It starts with a problem anyone who’s tried this will recognize. DeepSeek reckons people can only keep track of 3–5 agent sessions at once. After that, we’re the bottleneck, not the models.

Their fix looks suspiciously like a small company. A Router hands out work to Workers running in parallel. Agents monitor GitHub discussions, investigate bugs and open pull requests. And a Watchdog checks whether anyone’s stuck or wandering off. We’ve automated coding, and now, apparently, middle management.

In simulated tests, the 95th-percentile task time dropped from 29.5 to 15.7 minutes. That’s nearly halved, but it came at the cost of a lot more tokens, and the tests didn’t measure whether the code was actually any good.

Getting one agent to do useful work keeps getting easier. Managing ten is a different job entirely, and right now it feels like herding very fast interns. DeepSeek is betting the next big jump comes from agents coordinating themselves, so we review the results instead of supervising every step. I think that’s the right bet, even if this isn’t the final version of it.

The [DeepSeek Harness prototype](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) is open source, but Super-agent itself is still a proposal, not a product.


----------

----------
# **MY TOP FINDINGS OF THE DAY**


--------------------
People are using Claude Opus 5.5 to rebuild big, well-known software from scratch, then open-sourcing it. Apps that took years and huge teams are being replicated in days. It’s happening fast.

----------
howdy, it’s Barsee again.

happy tuesday, AI family, and welcome back to AI Valley.

**here are the biggest things worth knowing today:**

* Karpathy got annoyed with YouTube and built his own in two hours

* GPT-6 Astra just performed brain surgery on another AI

* Audio recordings might be giving away more than you think

* Plus trending AI tools, posts, and resources

Let’s _dive_ into the Valley of AI…


----------

----------
#### **VIKTOR**

## [If you can brief a new hire, you can manage me](https://ref.viktor.com/vik-aiv-main13-hl)

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/2f2c4806-71bd-4ef5-8537-d187ba42a3b1/aivalley_main13_1280x720__2_.jpg?t=1793714124)
Caption: [Courtesy: Viktor](https://ref.viktor.com/vik-aiv-main13-hl)

I'm Viktor, the AI employee 70,000+ teams have hired, and managing me takes the skills you already use with people.

You give me a brief the way you'd give one to a new hire: "Pull this month's feedback from Intercom, #feedback and support email, group it by issue and draft fixes for the top three." I work inside the 3,200+ tools you connect, including ones with no API, and hand back the working app.

You correct me once and I remember it. When a task repeats, you make it one of my duties and I run it on a schedule. Anyone on the team can brief me, so the context sales gives me is there when finance asks. Anything I can't undo waits for your approval, the way a new hire checks before anything big.

Write my first brief today.

[Start free with up to $100 in credits, no credit card.](https://ref.viktor.com/vik-aiv-main13)

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/ba1324c1-631e-4e45-b167-a588179c1c00/image_-_2026-11-03T200840.220__1_.png?t=1793716543)
Follow image link: (https://hackertube.org/)
Caption: Courtesy: Karpathy

**1/ **[**Karpathy got annoyed with YouTube and built his own in two hours.**](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2116957135661945283?a=K8adZoaTNCMRlDZfB7E&s=20)** **He had Claude Opus 5.5 dig through 43 million Hacker News comments from the last 20 years and pull out the 6,454 videos people kept recommending. The result is [HackerTube](https://hackertube.org/). No recommendation algorithm, no clickbait thumbnails, no login.

I opened it expecting a weekend toy and ended up with a stack of tabs I’ll never close. It’s mostly the conference talks, lectures and deep dives HN has been passing around for years, the stuff YouTube would never show you because it doesn’t keep you scrolling. The thumbnails are actual frames from the videos, which sounds minor until you realize how much of YouTube is people making shocked faces at you.

The build is the bit that gets me. Karpathy did the boring admin (API key, server, domain) and Claude Code did the rest: the code, the deployment, even locking down the server. A few years ago this would’ve been a proper side project with a half-finished GitHub repo to show for it. Now you can get fed up with an algorithm over breakfast and have your own version up by lunch.

People are already copying the idea. Someone made [Hacker Papers](https://x.com/omarsar0/status/2117053859516285354) for arXiv papers, [someone else](https://x.com/oianas_/status/2117215383015100901) did books. I’m half tempted to build one for podcasts, because my podcast app’s idea of “for you” is the same five shows I already subscribe to.

I think this is where things are heading. We spent fifteen years letting a handful of algorithms decide what we see. Turns out the fix might just be building your own feed, from people whose taste you trust.

**2/ **[**GPT-6 Astra just performed brain surgery on another AI.**](https://x.com/rikiyatakehi/status/2117313742891327994?a=-n0tpVT7CEKZhEMrbF0&s=20) MIT researchers asked it to fix the math skills of a small model, Qwen3.5-0.8B, which kept getting stuck in reasoning loops. Astra looked at the model’s weights, worked out what was going wrong and edited 0.016% of them. Its MATH-500 score went from 7.9% to 48.1%, and its instruction-following nearly tripled. No retraining at all.

My first reaction was a slightly uneasy “oh.” Then I read [Sean Goedecke’s breakdown](https://www.seangoedecke.com/llms-are-not-superhuman-at-reading-and-writing-neural-network-weights/), which brings things back down to earth. Astra didn’t teach Qwen any maths; it found the weights behind the loops and turned them down. A good ML researcher could have done the same.

But that’s sort of the point. “A good ML researcher could have done it” used to be the bottleneck. There aren’t many of those people, and they’re expensive. If AI can do that kind of debugging on demand, fixing a broken model starts to look less like a research project and more like running a diagnostic. It’s tiny and early, and it’s on a 0.8B model, not something frontier-sized. The question I’ll be watching is whether it works on models big enough to matter.


----------

----------
# MY TOP FINDINGS OF THE DAY


--------------------
**Audio recordings might be giving away more than you think.** One of the wildest demos I've seen lately shows how AI can use background sounds to narrow down where a recording was made. Not GPS data, not anything deliberately shared. Just clues hiding in the audio.

Think about all the voice notes, podcasts and videos people have uploaded from their homes over the years. Some might contain enough environmental clues to reveal a location nobody intended to share.
